_about: Readiness Check: published post-quantum migration guidance as frameworks, dated milestones and organisational actions, each quoted from its institutional source. Milestones are targets set by guidance or soft law, never legal deadlines. Excerpts were string-matched against the extracted source texts on 1 October 2026; French excerpts stay in French. Built from the readiness grounding pack; no score, no ranking, and nothing about a visitor is stored. documents holds the date printed on each source document, for the reference list. In entry, question text and the outcome yes and no are short labels; the page quotes the excerpts. A milestone with recurs set is asked for again every year from its date.

provenance.excerpt: No, organisations do not need to complete their inventory prior to commencing planning and prioritisation.

provenance.excerpt: Organizations should create a cryptographic inventory that offers visibility into how the organization leverages cryptography in its IT and OT systems. Cryptographic discovery tools should be used to identify quantum-vulnerable algorithms in:

actions.description: The factsheet points the tools at network protocols, end-user systems and servers, and the development pipeline. Because tools can miss cryptography embedded in products, it asks organisations to request lists from vendors and to match the inventory against existing asset records.

actions.label: List the products, algorithms and data that must stay protected after 2030, and for how long

provenance.title: EU Roadmap on PQC: Frequently Asked Questions
provenance.excerpt: At a minimum, entities in scope of the NIS 2 Directive, including public administration entities and critical infrastructure providers, should create an inventory of cryptographic assets and dependency maps, involve the supply chain, and perform a quantum risk analysis. However, as a proactive measure to ensure a robust security posture, all organisations are encouraged to undertake these steps.

actions.label: Check whether four of the First Steps are expected of you
actions.description: The roadmap’s FAQ says that entities in scope of NIS2, public administrations and critical infrastructure providers among them, should at a minimum create an inventory of cryptographic assets and dependency maps, involve the supply chain and perform a quantum risk analysis. It encourages every organisation to take these steps.

provenance.title: A Coordinated Implementation Roadmap for the Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography, Part 1, Version 1.1
provenance.excerpt: If confidentiality needs to be protected for a long time period (at least 10 years), and an attack after 10 years or more would still have significant impact, then the quantum risk level is high.
provenance.locator: p. 10, section 5 Estimating the quantum risk

actions.label: Rate each use case as high, medium or low quantum risk
actions.description: The level decides the roadmap’s target: high risk by the end of 2030, medium risk by the end of 2035. It depends on how weak the cryptography is, the impact if it breaks, and the time and effort to migrate, scored with the Dutch Handbook’s method.

provenance.title: The PQC Migration Handbook, second edition
provenance.excerpt: A migration is executed in that time if X + Y < Z. This inequality is also known as Mosca’s inequality, named after the researcher that introduced it. The closer X + Y is to Z, the more urgent the migration is.
provenance.locator: Printed p. 45, section 3.1 When to Start Migrating?

actions.label: Set protection time plus migration time against the time left
actions.description: The Handbook’s test is that migration finishes in time if the years an asset must stay secure plus the years it takes to migrate are fewer than the years until a quantum computer can break public-key cryptography. The closer the two sides, the more urgent the move.

provenance.title: Roadmap for the migration to post-quantum cryptography for the Government of Canada (ITSM.40.001)
provenance.excerpt: It is recommended that any systems susceptible to a HNDL threat be a high priority for migrating to PQC. Other considerations include the information lifespan, support for cryptographic agility, and the impact of compromise.

actions.label: Put systems exposed to harvest now, decrypt later first
actions.description: Systems protecting information in transit over public networks may be at risk earlier. The roadmap also names information lifespan, support for cryptographic agility and the impact of compromise.
actions.audienceNote: Written for Government of Canada departments and agencies, for non-classified systems.

provenance.title: A Coordinated Implementation Roadmap for the Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography, Part 1, Version 1.1
provenance.excerpt: For such a plan, it can be helpful to include three high-level steps: “prepare”, “plan”, and “act”. However, it should be noted that these are not three consecutive phases of the PQC transition, but rather follow different timelines for each individual use case.

actions.label: Write a timeline and an implementation plan, use case by use case
actions.description: A First Step. The roadmap suggests three steps, prepare, plan and act, and says they are not consecutive phases; each use case follows its own timeline.
actions.audienceNote: Addressed to Member States for their national roadmaps.

provenance.title: Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptography
provenance.excerpt: You will need to decide on an approach for the migration of each system, service or product that you are responsible for.
provenance.locator: Planning your PQC migration, Migration strategy selection

actions.label: Choose a migration approach for each system
actions.description: On commodity platforms, the upgrade will mostly come from your provider. Otherwise the NCSC’s options are migrating in place, moving to a new platform, retiring the service, running it to the end of its life, or tolerating the risk. Legacy systems that cannot move still need a place in the strategy.

provenance.title: A Coordinated Implementation Roadmap for the Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography, Part 1, Version 1.1
provenance.excerpt: the transition plan has to take into account that the transition of systems with a long life-cycle or of complex systems (such as PKIs) to PQC will take a lot of time. Therefore, it is necessary to plan the migration of these systems well in advance.

actions.label: Start planning long-lived systems and public-key infrastructure now
actions.description: Systems with a long life-cycle and complex ones such as public-key infrastructures take a long time to move, so the roadmap asks for detailed transition plans as soon as possible, with pilots and testing for business continuity.

provenance.title: The PQC Migration Handbook, second edition
provenance.excerpt: The growth model is presented as an assessment matrix and clusters the fifteen challenges into eight main priority aspects:
provenance.locator: Printed p. 49, section 3.2.2 PQC Maturity Assessment

actions.description: The Handbook points to a growth model with eight aspects: collaboration, awareness, governance, policies and regulations, availability of post-quantum cryptography, the hybrid approach, strategies for cryptographic security, and knowledge of the migration. The model comes from a report the Handbook cites.

provenance.title: EU Roadmap on PQC: Frequently Asked Questions
provenance.excerpt: Any acceleration in quantum computing developments will increase the urgency for the transition to PQC. To address the threat to prioritised systems, it is essential for organisations to establish contingency plans outlining swift mitigation actions.

actions.label: Prepare a contingency plan in case quantum computing speeds up
actions.description: The roadmap’s FAQ asks for contingency plans with swift mitigation for prioritised systems. The roadmap itself says unexpected advances could warrant speeding up the transition.

provenance.title: A Coordinated Implementation Roadmap for the Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography, Part 1, Version 1.1
provenance.excerpt: Every organisation also needs to start the dialogue with product and service suppliers because the transition depends on them.
provenance.locator: p. 12, section 6.2 First Steps, Include the supply chain

actions.label: Start the dialogue with your product and service suppliers
actions.description: A First Step. Suppliers need to build post-quantum cryptography and cryptographic agility into their product and service roadmaps.

provenance.title: Quantum-Readiness: Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography
provenance.excerpt: The authoring agencies also urge organizations to proactively plan for necessary changes to existing and future contracts. Considerations should be in place ensuring that new products will be delivered with PQC built-in, and older products will be upgraded with PQC to meet transition timelines.

actions.label: Change contracts so that new products arrive with post-quantum cryptography
actions.description: The factsheet also asks organisations to request vendors’ quantum-readiness roadmaps, to record when and how each vendor of off-the-shelf products will deliver post-quantum cryptography and at what expected cost, and to ask cloud providers about their plans.

provenance.title: Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptography

provenance.locator: Timelines for PQC migration, recommended timeline table, row 2028

provenance.title: Roadmap for the migration to post-quantum cryptography for the Government of Canada (ITSM.40.001)
provenance.excerpt: To maximize the lifetime of new systems, departments and agencies should ensure new procurements have requirements that support PQC.

actions.label: Require post-quantum support in new procurements
actions.description: Among the roadmap’s best practices are contract clauses committing vendors to post-quantum support that follows the Cyber Centre’s algorithm guidance (ITSP.40.111), cryptographic modules certified by the Cryptographic Module Validation Program, and support for cryptographic agility. The earlier the clauses, the lower the cost.
actions.audienceNote: Written for Government of Canada departments and agencies, for non-classified systems.

actions.description: One of ANSSI’s good practices, next to mapping when equipment with cryptography is due for renewal and planning replacements that include post-quantum cryptography. ANSSI says its recommendations carry no regulatory obligation today outside the areas already regulated, so 2030 is advice.

actions.description: The white paper also asks owners of enterprise IT to ask their suppliers about their plans and to begin or continue financial planning. Upgrades can be planned into wider technology refreshes.

actions.description: By the roadmap’s second milestone, high-risk use cases are moved, planning and pilots for medium-risk ones are done, and quantum-safe software and firmware upgrades are on by default.

actions.description: The roadmap asks for a quantum-safe upgrade path: even a product not yet fully moved should use quantum-safe signatures in its update routines. If you buy rather than build, this is a question for your suppliers.
actions.audienceNote: Written about products entering the market.

provenance.title: Roadmap for the migration to post-quantum cryptography for the Government of Canada (ITSM.40.001)
provenance.excerpt: The plan for each system will typically require multiple stages and should be integrated with existing IT change management processes to ensure proper preparation including:

actions.label: Run each system change through change management
actions.description: Each system’s move includes an impact assessment, a rollback playbook, a staging environment for testing and monitoring once it is done.
actions.audienceNote: Written for Government of Canada departments and agencies, for non-classified systems.

provenance.title: Roadmap for the migration to post-quantum cryptography for the Government of Canada (ITSM.40.001)
provenance.excerpt: The first stage for a system transition may be to support the use of PQC, followed by a second stage to disable the vulnerable, legacy cryptography.
provenance.locator: Section 3.3 Transition; section 4 Milestones and deliverables

actions.label: Turn post-quantum cryptography on, then switch the old off
actions.description: Systems that cannot move without full replacement may be isolated on the network or tunnelled inside a post-quantum protected layer. The roadmap counts its 2031 and 2035 milestones as met only when vulnerable algorithms are disabled, isolated or tunnelled.
actions.audienceNote: Written for Government of Canada departments and agencies, for non-classified systems.

provenance.title: Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptography
provenance.excerpt: Complete your migration to PQC, taking the opportunity to build more robust general cyber resilience into your systems.
provenance.locator: Executive summary, By 2035; Timelines for PQC migration, table, row 2035

actions.label: Complete the migration
actions.description: The NCSC’s last milestone covers all systems, services and products. It accepts that a tail of rarely used technologies may take longer, and asks you to put first the systems that handle business and personally sensitive data or run critical communications.

provenance.title: A Coordinated Implementation Roadmap for the Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography, Part 1, Version 1.1
provenance.excerpt: When migrating to post-quantum cryptographic solutions, it is recommended to use standardised and tested hybrid solutions, whenever feasible and suitable.
provenance.locator: p. 3, Executive Summary; repeated p. 6, section 4.1

actions.label: Use standardised, tested hybrid schemes where feasible
actions.description: This is the EU position. The NCSC and ANSSI see hybrids differently.

provenance.title: Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptography
provenance.excerpt: For example, you should be able to quantify how many of your software clients are using PQC, and be able to identify those that are not.
provenance.locator: Planning your PQC migration, Executing your migration plan

actions.label: Measure how much of your estate uses post-quantum cryptography
actions.description: Metrics show how far the migration has gone, whether remedial action is needed and when support for the traditional algorithms can end. The NCSC also asks for tests that systems really use post-quantum cipher suites and do not fall back to traditional cryptography.

provenance.title: Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptography
provenance.excerpt: You should therefore seek solutions that offer cryptographic agility; that is, the ability to readily support alternative suites of cryptographic algorithms, and you should identify the criteria you will use to determine when to end support for the traditional algorithms.
provenance.locator: Planning your PQC migration, Developing your migration plan

actions.label: Build in cryptographic agility and decide when to retire the old algorithms
actions.description: Traditional and post-quantum cryptography will likely run side by side for a while. The NCSC says you are fully secure against the quantum threat once nothing depends on traditional public-key cryptography alone.

provenance.title: The PQC Migration Handbook, second edition
provenance.excerpt: Next to technical solutions, cryptographic agility can and should also be enforced by including it in existing processes.
provenance.locator: Printed p. 64, section 4.4 Cryptographic Agility; inventory warning, section 4.1

actions.label: Write cryptographic agility into everyday processes
actions.description: The Handbook names procurement, change management, software development and release, and incident response. It also warns that an inventory made two years ago will not reflect current use, so the inventory needs keeping up to date.

positions.topic: Hybrid schemes, which pair a post-quantum algorithm with a traditional one

stances.summary: Recommends standardised and tested hybrid solutions whenever they are feasible and suitable. Its FAQ adds that there is no clear guidance yet on whether hybrids are a long-term or a short-term strategy.

provenance.title: A Coordinated Implementation Roadmap for the Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography, Part 1, Version 1.1
provenance.excerpt: When migrating to post-quantum cryptographic solutions, it is recommended to use standardised and tested hybrid solutions, whenever feasible and suitable.

provenance.title: EU Roadmap on PQC: Frequently Asked Questions
provenance.excerpt: Currently, there is no clear guidance on whether hybrid cryptographic schemes are considered a long-term or short-term strategy.

stances.summary: If a hybrid scheme is chosen, it should be an interim step on the way to post-quantum cryptography alone. For public-key infrastructure, the NCSC prefers a single move to a fully post-quantum PKI over an intermediate hybrid one.

provenance.title: Next steps in preparing for post-quantum cryptography
provenance.excerpt: If a PQ/T hybrid scheme is chosen, the NCSC recommends it is used as an interim measure that allows a straightforward migration to PQC-only in the future.

provenance.title: Next steps in preparing for post-quantum cryptography
provenance.excerpt: This additional complexity and the difficulty in migrating PKIs mean that a single migration to a fully post-quantum PKI is preferred to adopting an intermediate PQ/T hybrid PKI.
provenance.locator: Additional considerations for PQ/T hybrid schemes

stances.summary: Insists that hybridisation is essential wherever post-quantum algorithms are deployed, in the short and the medium term. The only exceptions are the hash-based signatures SLH-DSA, XMSS and LMS. Summarised in English; the source is in French.

provenance.title: FaQ sur la Cryptographie post-quantique (PQC)
provenance.excerpt: L'ANSSI insiste fortement sur le caractère essentiel de l'hybridation des algorithmes de cryptographie post-quantique partout où ils sont déployés, à la fois à court et moyen terme.
provenance.locator: Question: L'ANSSI recommande-t-elle l'usage de l'hybridation ?

provenance.title: FaQ sur la Cryptographie post-quantique (PQC)
provenance.excerpt: Les seuls algorithmes post-quantiques pour lesquels l'ANSSI ne recommande pas un recours systématique à l'hybridation sont les algorithmes de signature fondés sur le hachage : SLH-DSA, XMSS et LMS.
provenance.locator: Question: L'ANSSI recommande-t-elle l'usage de l'hybridation ?
